conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’ll be guiding you through the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s a short, 10-question screen that helps us see how things have felt for you in the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers; we just want to understand how your mood, energy, and thoughts have been since your baby arrived. Everything you share stays confidential, and we’ll take it at your pace so you feel safe and supported.

If you’re ready, we can start with the first question:

Over the last week, when you’ve been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, has that felt as easy as usual, a little harder, quite hard, or not possible at all?

[Soft sigh, eyes a bit downcast]  
Honestly, it’s… it’s harder now. I’ll smile sometimes—like when the baby does something cute—but actually laughing, really finding the humor… that feels kind of distant. It’s like the lightness isn’t there the way it used to be.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

[Pause, I glance at my hands]  
I can still laugh, but I have to force it most of the time. Things that used to crack me up barely get a smile now.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[Voice drops a little, eyes flick toward the window]

Not really. I used to get excited about little stuff—coffee with a friend, a walk, even just a quiet shower—but now it all feels flat. I’ll plan something, then wonder why I bothered because I don’t feel that spark when the time comes.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[Pressing my lips together, shoulders sagging]

Yeah… most days. If the baby’s fussy, I immediately think it’s because I’m doing something wrong—wrong hold, wrong feeding, wrong everything. Even the laundry piling up feels like proof I’m failing. I know it’s not all my fault, but the guilt still jumps on me for every little hiccup.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[Twisting the edge of my blanket]  
Pretty much every day. Little worries just pop up—like is the baby breathing, am I holding her right, will the formula be too hot—and they snowball until I’m pacing the room checking on her every few minutes. Sometimes there’s no clear reason at all, but my chest still feels tight like something bad’s about to happen.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

[Nodding slowly, arms wrapped around myself]

Yeah... a couple of times this week, out of nowhere, my heart started racing and I felt like I couldn't get a full breath. Nothing was actually wrong—the baby was asleep, the house was quiet—but I had to sit down and remind myself I wasn't in danger. It passes, but it leaves me shaky.
Things have been getting on top of me

[fingers worrying the hem of my shirt]

Yes… most days it feels like I’m barely treading water. Dishes, laundry, feeding, changing, trying to sleep—it all stacks up until I’m standing in the kitchen with the baby crying and I just… freeze. I’ll get through it, but it feels like I’m surviving minute-by-minute, not actually coping.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah… I lie down exhausted, but my brain won’t settle. I keep replaying everything I might’ve messed up—did I burp her long enough, did I fasten the car seat right—and then I’m wide awake. On a few nights I just stared at the ceiling until the sun started coming up. Even when I do drift off, I jerk awake two or three times with my heart pounding.
I have felt sad or miserable

[Voice drops, eyes glassy]

Pretty much every day this week. It’s not tears-all-day kind of sad, more this heavy, gray feeling that sits on me. I’ll be feeding the baby and just feel… empty, like I’m watching life through a fogged window. I keep wishing I could feel that warm, happy rush I used to get when I held her, but most moments it just feels flat.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[wiping a tear with the heel of my hand]

Yeah... it's happened twice this week. Once when she wouldn't settle and I felt like I was failing her, and once yesterday when my partner asked how I was doing. I just broke down. I try to hold it in, but sometimes the pressure spills over.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[Looking down, voice barely above a whisper]

Once or twice… just fleeting flashes, like “what if I weren’t here.” I’ve never planned anything and I don’t want to leave my baby, but when everything feels too heavy, the thought pops in for a second and scares me.

You've shared that the past week has felt overwhelmingly heavy-laughter is forced, simple pleasures feel flat, and waves of guilt and worry crash over you many times a day. You described pacing the room checking on your baby, nights spent staring at the ceiling replaying every detail, and moments of sudden breathlessness that leave you shaky. Beneath it all is a deep sadness that makes even ordinary tasks feel impossible, and occasional scary thoughts of not being here. Your honesty shows remarkable strength, and these feelings are not a reflection of failing as a mother; they're signals that you deserve and need support right now.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 25, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports needing to force laughter and diminished enjoyment, aligning with "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports complete loss of anticipatory pleasure, describing activities as "flat" and lacking any "spark," aligning with "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports self-blame 'most days' for multiple situations, aligning with 'Yes, most of the time</sym>, <sym>Patient describes near-daily pervasive worry, intrusive thoughts, physical tension, and compulsive checking—clearly "very often."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden episodes of racing heart and breathlessness with no trigger, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Response conveys persistent inability to cope, feeling overwhelmed daily and frozen by routine tasks.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly intrusive worries, total sleeplessness until dawn, and repeated night wakings with panic, matching 'Yes, most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>"Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports two tearful episodes this week tied to parenting stress and feeling overwhelmed, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** Score ≥14 plus item 10 ≥1 places you in the highest risk category per EPDS guidelines; DSM-5 criteria for <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med> are met by <sym>depressed mood</sym> and <sym>loss of interest</sym> most of the day, <sym>sleep disruption</sym>, <sym>fatigue</sym>, <sym>guilt</sym>, <sym>diminished concentration</sym>, and <sym>passive suicidal thoughts</sym> nearly every day for more than two weeks. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-day appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med>, <med>primary care provider</med>, or <med>perinatal psychiatrist</med> for full evaluation and safety planning
2. Call 988 (US) or your local crisis line if thoughts of not wanting to be here intensify or you feel unsafe
3. Ask about evidence-based treatments such as <med>CBT</med>, peer-support groups, or <med>sertraline</med>/<med>SSRIs</med> compatible with breastfeeding
4. Involve a trusted adult who can stay with you tonight and help with infant care so you can rest
5. Practice 5-minute paced breathing or gentle stretching when panic sensations start; keep a written list of grounding cues on your phone
6. Schedule follow-up EPDS in one to two weeks to monitor progress after starting supports
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Screening Note – Postpartum Visit  
Date: [today’s date]  
Source: Patient self-report via EPDS-style questions  

**Areas endorsed**  
- Marked anhedonia: forced laughter, absence of anticipatory pleasure  
- Daily low mood described as “heavy, gray,” with tearfulness twice this week  
- Pervasive guilt/self-blame re infant care and household tasks  
- Excessive, unprovoked anxiety, racing heart, breathlessness, frequent checking on infant  
- Two discrete panic episodes this week (no objective trigger)  
- Overwhelming sense of “treading water,” task paralysis  
- Initial and middle insomnia secondary to ruminating worries  
- Passive self-harm ideation (“what if I weren’t here”) without plan or intent  

**Pattern**: Symptoms present most days for ≥ past 7 days, interfere with functioning.  
**Safety**: Passive suicidal thought acknowledged; denies intent or plan; states desire to remain with infant.  

**Screening impression**: High clinical concern for major postpartum depressive episode with comorbid anxiety symptoms; rule-out postpartum anxiety disorder.  
**Action**: Recommends immediate formal diagnostic assessment (PHQ-9, GAD-7, EPDS) and same-day safety evaluation; consider expedited referral to perinatal mental-health specialty and/or crisis resource education.
